plan.question: Will a desperate soldier's plea for mercy survive the brutal calculus of war?

chapters.title: A Fatal Precedent
beats: In the final winter of the Second World War, American forces faced a crisis of discipline as tens of thousands of soldiers deserted during brutal combat against Germany across Western Europe.
Military authorities processed over one million courts-martial to maintain order on the battlefield, creating a tension between systemic military deterrence and individual justice.
A single American soldier was singled out to face the ultimate penalty, breaking a historical precedent that had stood since the American Civil War.
The decision brought high-ranking commanders, military lawyers, and frontline officers into a moral struggle over whether execution was a necessary military deterrent or an unnecessary tragedy.

chapters.title: The Draftee and the General
beats: Edward Donald Slovik, a troubled youth from Detroit, Michigan with a criminal record, sought a quiet life after marrying Antoinette Wisniewski, but found himself drafted into the U.S. Army as a replacement rifleman bound for France.

Dwight D. Eisenhower, Supreme Allied Commander, held supreme responsibility for maintaining order and morale across millions of Allied troops advancing through Western Europe against desperate German counterattacks.
Norman Cota, a veteran frontline major general, commanded the military division desperately in need of replacements to sustain its bloody offensive through heavily defended European battlefields.
Ralph Grotte, a frontline captain responsible for leading Company G in brutal infantry combat, stood direct guard over the discipline and survival of his rifle platoons.
Antoinette Wisniewski remained in Detroit, Michigan, fighting to save her husband from his troubled past and later striving to redeem his name and restore his memory.

The vital strategic conflict centered on France, where Allied forces fought to break German resistance, turning every frontline unit into a crucial stronghold where desertion threatened to collapse troop morale.

chapters.title: From Detroit to the Front
beats: Born in Detroit, Michigan in 1920, Edward Donald Slovik struggled through a delinquent youth, enduring repeated arrests for stealing brass and joyriding before securing parole and marrying Antoinette Wisniewski in late 1942.

Reclassified by the military, Edward Donald Slovik was drafted in early 1944, undergoing infantry training before being dispatched to France as part of a replacement group assigned to a frontline infantry division.

En route to his designated unit near Elbeuf, France, Edward Donald Slovik and a companion took cover during an intense artillery attack and became separated from their unit, temporarily staying with a military police detachment.

Upon returning to his unit in October 1944, Edward Donald Slovik directly informed Captain Ralph Grotte that he was too terrified to serve in a front-line rifle platoon and requested reassignment to a rear unit.
When Ralph Grotte refused the request and sent him to a rifle platoon anyway, Edward Donald Slovik immediately deserted his unit, turning himself in shortly after with a signed written confession.
chapters.hook: His written confession made a trial inevitable, but no one expected the sentence to be fatal.

chapters.title: The Death Sentence
beats: On November 11, 1944, a court-martial of nine officers tried Edward Donald Slovik in France, convicting him of desertion to avoid hazardous duty and sentencing him to death.

Major General Norman Cota reviewed the trial record and approved the death sentence, believing that executing a deserter was vital to deter other frontline soldiers from abandoning their posts under fire.
From his prison cell, Edward Donald Slovik wrote a direct appeal to Supreme Allied Commander Dwight D. Eisenhower on December 9, pleading for clemency and asking for his life to be spared.
On December 16, a massive surprise German offensive struck the Ardennes, sparking the fierce Battle of the Bulge and causing thousands of American casualties and severe manpower shortages.
Faced with rising desertion numbers during the desperate battle, Dwight D. Eisenhower personally confirmed the execution order on December 23, sealing Edward Donald Slovik's fate.

chapters.title: Execution at Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines
beats: On the morning of January 31, 1945, in Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France, military guards led Edward Donald Slovik to a courtyard set up for his execution.
A firing squad composed of twelve soldiers drawn from his assigned regiment stood assembled, facing the bound prisoner with loaded rifles.
Refusing to abandon his belief that his punishment was unmerited, Edward Donald Slovik remarked that his mind was made up as he prepared to face the rifles.

At 10:04 a.m., the command was given, and eleven bullets struck Edward Donald Slovik, making him the only American soldier executed for desertion during World War II out of 21,000 sentenced deserters.
Following his execution, the military buried Edward Donald Slovik in Plot E of a French cemetery alongside 95 American soldiers executed for murder or rape.

chapters.title: The Aftermath and the Fight for Redemption
beats: In the summer of 1945, a military clemency board reviewed thousands of courts-martial sentences, freeing thousands of convicted soldiers while Edward Donald Slovik's execution stood untouched.
Antoinette Wisniewski spent decades petitioning U.S. presidents for a pardon, seeking her husband's withheld pension and demanding the return of his physical remains until her death in 1979.
Author William Bradford Huie published the book The Execution of Private Slovik in 1954, bringing the hidden story of the court-martial into national public debate.
In 1974, a television movie adaptation starring Martin Sheen brought the story of Edward Donald Slovik's execution to millions of American viewers.
In 1987, President Ronald Reagan ordered the return of Edward Donald Slovik's remains, allowing them to be exhumed from France and reburied in Detroit, Michigan.
